name: Freya Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for talking to me, Freya. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to AI companies, employers, unions or any party, and everything here is confidential. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I do lettings and property management at Marsh Property, a family-run agency in a market town. Most days I'm out doing inventories and check-outs, going round a house with a clipboard and a camera, noting every scuff and stain. Then I'm back in the office arranging plumbers and electricians for the hundred and twenty homes we manage. It's a lot of driving and a lot of phone calls.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what gets to you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that I know every house and every landlord. I can tell you which boiler in Church Lane makes a noise before it dies. What gets to me is the deposit fights at the end of a tenancy, where both sides think I'm on the other side. And the pay, which is low, because my boss Mr Marsh says the margins are thin. My boyfriend Dan works nights picking orders at the big warehouse off the bypass.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, because people round here have been promising computers would change everything since I started. I'd say good, maybe now everyone can calm down. I don't really post things, so it'd be a chat in the office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it doesn't change much. Nothing changing doesn't mean fine. My boss Mr Marsh is sixty-six and keeps talking about selling up, and a chain would want fewer of us. That worry was there before any AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job and keep my head down. I'd cut back where I can, no new car, no holiday this year. I'd probably also ask Mr Marsh straight out what his plans are, which I've been putting off for months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but it's a familiar worry, if that makes sense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Mr Marsh is the owner. How long does he plan to keep going?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He says two more years, but he's said that for three years. His daughter doesn't want the business. If a chain like the one in the next town buys us, they run lettings from a central office and send out someone cheaper to do the inventories.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your money look like month to month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We've got about two or three weeks' money saved. My car is old and the clutch is going, and I need the car for the job. If it goes, that's the savings gone in one go.

say: I'd say I'm **not surprised**, because the big promises never came true.
I'd tell the office everyone can **calm down** now.
think: Nothing changing isn't the same as **fine**, because the owner may **sell up**.
A **chain** buying us would mean fewer staff and cheaper inventory clerks.
do: Skip a **new car** and a holiday this year to protect savings.
Ask **Mr Marsh** directly about his plans for the business.
feel: She feels **worried**, though it's a **familiar** worry.
S0.quote: Nothing changing doesn't mean fine. My boss Mr Marsh is sixty-six and keeps talking about selling up, and a chain would want fewer of us.
fieldNote: Freya's main risk is the **owner retiring**, a pressure that predates AI.
Her car is a **single point** of failure for both job and savings.
She avoids hard conversations, but would finally ask her **boss** about his plans.

steps.text: Hold off on a new car and skip this year's holiday
Keep doing inventories and check-outs at Marsh Property

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a bit much, but people will adapt like they always do. I'd probably say the office still needs someone who knows the houses. I'd keep it practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the office work goes first. Booking contractors, answering tenants, writing the adverts, chasing rent, that's all on your list. If I only do the driving bit, they could pay me less or give it to a cheaper person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait a bit to see what Mr Marsh actually does before I panic. I'd keep doing the inventories well, because that's the bit where you need someone on the floor. And I'd stop putting anything on the credit card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, and a bit stubborn about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You don't use AI tools at all. What happens if Marsh Property brings them in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to avoid it as long as I could, honestly. I'd let Kerry in the office learn it, and I'd stay on the houses. But I know that only works until somebody notices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of your job feels safest?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The inventories and check-outs. You've got to be in the room to see a burn mark on a worktop or smell that someone's had a dog. A computer can't do that from a desk, at least not in this picture.

say: I'd say it's **a bit much**, but people adapt.
I'd remind everyone the office needs someone who **knows the houses**.
think: The **office work** goes first: contractors, tenant calls, adverts and rent chasing.
Doing only the **driving bit**, I could be paid less or replaced cheaper.
do: Wait to see what **Mr Marsh** does before making changes.
Stop using the **credit card** and focus on doing inventories well.
feel: She feels **uneasy** and a bit **stubborn** about it.
S1.quote: You've got to be in the room to see a burn mark on a worktop or smell that someone's had a dog.
fieldNote: She clings to the **hands-on** inventory work as her safe ground.
She'd let a **colleague** learn AI rather than learn it herself.
She knows her **avoidance** only works until someone notices.

steps.text: Wait to see what Mr Marsh does before changing anything
Stop using the credit card for anything

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say something has to be done, and I'd probably say the government should slow it down. I'm not one for big opinions, but this would be too fast for anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the office side of Marsh Property is gone within a year or so. The inventories might keep me going until the robots come, but a chain would just get tenants to film the house on their phone. Then I've got nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my mum if Dan and I could move back into her house for a while, to stop paying rent. I'd cut everything we don't need. I'd look for any job that's hands-on, maybe cleaning or doing end-of-tenancy work for a cleaning firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. I'd feel like the ground was moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Robots for hands-on work come about three years after AGI. What does that mean for the inventories?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In theory they buy me until 2031. In practice, I think the landlords would rather have a cheap video than pay me to drive out. So maybe a year more than the office girls, not three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And Dan's job at the warehouse?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the bit that really scares me. The warehouse is already half robots, and my boyfriend Dan says the new ones can pick almost anything. If we both go, there's nothing coming in.

say: I'd say the **government** should slow it down.
I'd say it's **too fast** for anyone to cope with.
think: The **office side** of Marsh Property would be gone within a year.
Tenant **phone videos** could replace my inventories before robots arrive.
do: Move back in with **my mum** with Dan to stop paying rent.
Look for **hands-on work** like end-of-tenancy cleaning.
feel: She feels **scared**, like the ground is moving.
S2.quote: The warehouse is already half robots, and my boyfriend Dan says the new ones can pick almost anything. If we both go, there's nothing coming in.
fieldNote: The household faces a **double hit**, since Dan's warehouse job is exposed too.
She expects only **a year** of extra time, not three.
Her instinct is to lean on **family**, not the state, for housing.

steps.text: Move into her mum's house with Dan to save rent
Ask her mum for help with housing for a while
Apply to end-of-tenancy cleaning firms for hands-on work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years sounds like a lot but it isn't. I'd tell friends to start saving and stop assuming someone will sort it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it's the same end for me, just slower. I'd be thirty-two with no savings and no other skills on paper. That's what keeps me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start putting fifty a month away, even if it's hard. I'd look at moving from inventories into property maintenance, maybe learning basic plumbing or tiling from the contractors I already book. By year three I'd want to be doing repairs, not paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, but at least I can see a road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in the first year of those five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the saving straight away. I'd ask Gary, the plumber we use most, if I could help him on Saturdays. He's always short of hands. That's where I'd learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the AI tools if it kept you on longer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if Mr Marsh made me. But I don't think it'd keep me on, it'd just mean I'm training the thing that does my job. I'd rather spend the time learning something with my hands.

say: I'd say **five years** sounds like a lot but isn't.
I'd tell friends to **start saving** now and not wait for help.
think: It's the **same end** for me, just a few years slower.
I'd be thirty-two with **no other skills** on paper.
do: Save **fifty a month** from now on, however hard.
Help **Gary the plumber** on Saturdays to learn maintenance work.
feel: She feels **alarmed**, but can now see a **road** ahead.
S3.quote: I'd ask Gary, the plumber we use most, if I could help him on Saturdays. He's always short of hands.
fieldNote: She'd move from **paperwork to repairs** using contractors she already knows.
She refuses to learn AI, seeing it as **training her replacement**.
Even with time, she expects to lose her current **role**.

steps.text: Put fifty a month into savings starting now
Help Gary the plumber on Saturdays to learn repairs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time, let's not panic. I'd tell people the young ones should get trades now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd probably wait too long. Ten years feels like forever and I'm not great at change. But I think I'd be all right if the maintenance side came together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job at Marsh Property while it lasts and keep saving a bit. I'd get to know the contractors and learn some basic repairs over the years. I'd wait and see for a while before doing anything big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Easier. Not calm, but easier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years. Does that let you breathe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. It's still there in the back of my head. The worry is like the clutch on my car: you know it'll go, but you don't know when.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be doing at thirty-seven?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe running my own little maintenance business with Dan, doing repairs for landlords I already know. That's a nice thought. But I'd need the robots not to beat me to it.

say: I'd say we've **got time** with ten years, so let's not panic.
I'd say **young people** should get trades now.
think: I'd probably **wait too long**, because I'm not great at change.
I'd be all right if the **maintenance side** came together.
do: Keep working at **Marsh Property** while the job lasts.
Learn **basic repairs** from contractors over the years and save a bit.
S4.quote: The worry is like the clutch on my car: you know it'll go, but you don't know when.
fieldNote: The decade gives her room to **delay**, and she knows it.
She pictures a **maintenance business** with Dan, a rare hopeful note.
Her plan still depends on **robots** arriving late.

steps.text: Wait a few years before making any big job change
Keep saving a small amount each month

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Dan and I would both be out and we've got nothing saved. What would help is time, really, and some way to learn a trade while still getting paid.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about who owns the agencies. When the small family places sell to the chains, that's when people like me get cut, AI or not.

headlineQuote: When the small family places sell to the chains, that's when people like me get cut, AI or not.
portrait: Freya is a **27-year-old** lettings and property manager at a family-run agency.
She lives with Dan, a **warehouse worker**, on two or three weeks of savings.
She's practical and **centrist**, never uses AI, and avoids hard conversations.
Her biggest fear is the owner **selling up**, which predates AI.
She'd move toward **repairs and maintenance** if given time.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most, because both she and Dan would be out of work.
whatWouldHelp: Time, and a way to **learn a trade** while still being paid.
